text: methods to study this, namely method of limits, method of constant stimulus, method of adjustment etc. In this experiment we will investigate the visual threshold to sense a spot of light using method of limits. This procedure allows for the external stimulus intensity to be displayed in an ascending and descending order depending on when the participants provide yes or no responses.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: in an ascending and descending order depending on when the participants provide yes or no responses. Based on participants responses a crossover point is generated by the software that provides the stimuli detection threshold in number of display steps. If the participant can detect the spot of light >50% of time, that intensity level would be considered as a visual threshold, according to method of limits.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: time, that intensity level would be considered as a visual threshold, according to method of limits. Method: Overview: The method of limits seeks to understand at what point an individual can detect a stimulus, and when they are no longer able to do so. The visual threshold to detect a spot of light using method of limits is the focus of the experiment.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: The visual threshold to detect a spot of light using method of limits is the focus of the experiment. To investigate the sensory threshold of our visual system we will run an online experiment on our desktops and provide detection responses using mouse clicks and keyboard. Participants: The study involved a single participant aged 27 years. This study was conducted at California State University, Bakersfield.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: single participant aged 27 years. This study was conducted at California State University, Bakersfield. Informed consent was obtained from the participant, who was informed of their right to withdraw from the study at any time. The participant had normal or corrected to normal vision. The participant did not have any medical conditions that would affect their participation in the experiment. Apparatus and stimuli: The experiment was conducted using the ISLE website, ISLE 2.2a.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: the experiment. Apparatus and stimuli: The experiment was conducted using the ISLE website, ISLE 2.2a. Method of limits (https://isle.hanover.edu/Ch02Methods/Ch02MethodOfLimits_evt.html ). I accessed this on a Dell desktop inside of computer lab 16 located in CSUB’s Walter Stern Library. The experiment settings were pre decided and were set in the browser manually, by moving the sliders for each setting value.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: were pre decided and were set in the browser manually, by moving the sliders for each setting value. Participants viewed the stimuli on a desktop computer with the monitor positioned at eye level. The stimuli consisted of a white dot measuring 4 pixels in diameter, presented 5 pixels above a red cross, which was located at the center of the screen. The background was grey with 100 units of display value intensity. The lowest intensity of dot was 1 unit while the highest was 50 units.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: units of display value intensity. The lowest intensity of dot was 1 unit while the highest was 50 units. The experiment comprised a total of 5 ascending and 5 descending staircases, with each staircase presenting the white dot of increasing or decreasing intensity, respectively. There were 5 repetitions for each intensity. Computer mouse was used to click yes or no as my response to each trial. Procedure: The light in the room were dimmed during the experiment run.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: as my response to each trial. Procedure: The light in the room were dimmed during the experiment run. Each trial began with participants fixating on a red cross at the center of the monitor. A white dot of varying intensity was then presented above the cross, and participants were prompted to respond "yes" (using the 'z' key) or "no" (using the '/' key) based on whether they perceived the dot. Participants completed the experiment in approximately 5 minutes.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: on whether they perceived the dot. Participants completed the experiment in approximately 5 minutes. The cross-over point occurred when the participant stated non-detection after a stream of detection and vice-versa. Every point of cross-over was averaged across all staircases to determine the participant’s threshold using this method. The experiment was run at a distance of 60 cm.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: determine the participant’s threshold using this method. The experiment was run at a distance of 60 cm. Result: The graph below (Figure 1) shows how the experiment ran over the course of the ascending and descending trails using staircase procedure. On the x-axis are the number of trails run and on the y-axis is the intensity/luminance of the dot that was displayed. The cross-over point is where the line changes direction.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

text: intensity/luminance of the dot that was displayed. The cross-over point is where the line changes direction. The data above shows that the visual threshold for me was 9.17 display steps. Figure 1: Trial sequence of the experiment using method of limits. Threshold is measured as a crossover point, when the response pattern change. This procedure utilized a staircase method to determine the crossover point of detection and non-detection. I found that my visual threshold of dot detection lies around 9.17 display steps, meaning that it would need this much difference between the background and the dot for me to detect it.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 0 method of limits\Lab 0 sample report.docx

This experiment illustrates the reliability and validity in quantifying visual thresholds.

This would affect the intensity values/detection thresholds, thus biasing the results.

If multiple hypothesis are tested, the probability of observing a rare event increases, and therefore, the likelihood of incorrectly rejecting a null hypothesis (i.e., making a Type I error) increases. The Bonferroni correction adjusts probability (p) values because of the increased risk of a type I error when making multiple statistical tests.

text: students in an outside financial interest. ❑ Cannot invest in business owned by subordinates or students. What Are Cognitive Biases? A cognitive bias is a systematic error in thinking that affects people’s decisions and judgments. In many instances, the flaw in judgment arises from memory errors, social attribution, and miscalculations.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\Refresher reserach and statistics.pdf

text: instances, the flaw in judgment arises from memory errors, social attribution, and miscalculations. Examples of Cognitive Biases Framing effect: The framing effect is a cognitive bias where people's decisions are influenced by how information is presented rather than the actual information itself. Survivorship Bias: Survivorship bias is a cognitive shortcut that occurs when a successful subgroup is mistaken as the entire group, due to the invisibility of the failure subgroup.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\Refresher reserach and statistics.pdf

text: successful subgroup is mistaken as the entire group, due to the invisibility of the failure subgroup. The bias name comes from the error an individual makes when a data set only considers the “surviving” observations, excluding points that didn't survive. Anchoring Bias: Anchoring bias is a cognitive bias where individuals rely too heavily on the first piece of information they receive (the anchor) when making decisions or estimates, even when that information may be irrelevant or misleading.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\Refresher reserach and statistics.pdf

text: anchor) when making decisions or estimates, even when that information may be irrelevant or misleading. Streetlight effect: The streetlight effect, or the drunkard's search principle, is a type of observational bias that occurs when people only search for something where it is easiest to look.

text: LL0: Understanding mental representations using mental rotation task Name Course University Many humans and even some animals can physically rotate and manipulate an object to make it match another stimulus or fit into a space. Examples of such activities can be seen in a child's shape sorting cube or the popular game Tetris. However, can one create a mental representation of a figure such as the letter "R" and rotate or manipulate it in our minds?
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\LL0\sample report LL0.docx

text: a mental representation of a figure such as the letter "R" and rotate or manipulate it in our minds? If so, can our response time and accuracy with the task be influenced by the mental representation orientation or its presentation, such as normal or reversed? Can one quantify and measure internal representations?
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\LL0\sample report LL0.docx

text: its presentation, such as normal or reversed? Can one quantify and measure internal representations? Studies such as Cooper and Shepard (1973) found that the response time increased the further the letter was from 0 to 360 degrees and was longer for mirror-imaged letters than normal letters. Therefore, it shows that both orientation and the image presentation affected response time and accuracy, whether normal or reversed.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\LL0\sample report LL0.docx

text: orientation and the image presentation affected response time and accuracy, whether normal or reversed. Additionally, the researchers could quantify and measure the participants' internal representations of the image through the study and data curation and analysis. The motivation for this experiment is to analyze how people interpret and understand visual information, specifically focusing on how individuals mentally rotate and recognize familiar shapes in various orientations.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\LL0\sample report LL0.docx

text: specifically focusing on how individuals mentally rotate and recognize familiar shapes in various orientations. This is important because it highlights how our brain processes visual information and understands objects. Showing how our brain perceives objects at different angles helps develop models of mental representations.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\LL0\sample report LL0.docx

text: how our brain perceives objects at different angles helps develop models of mental representations. In this experiment we conducted a variation of Cooper and Shepard (1973) study to set out to determine if orientation and stimuli presentation “Reversed” and “Normal” affects accuracy and response time. To determine this, we used two independent variables: Letter (Normal and Reversed) and Orientation (0, 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, 270, and 315).
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\LL0\sample report LL0.docx

text: independent variables: Letter (Normal and Reversed) and Orientation (0, 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, 270, and 315). We hypothesize that the Normal Letter condition will have a higher accuracy rate and quickest response times than the mirror reversed Letter conditions. We also predict that the 0-degree condition will have the highest accuracy and fastest response times, followed by 315 and 45 degrees.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\LL0\sample report LL0.docx

text: condition will have the highest accuracy and fastest response times, followed by 315 and 45 degrees. Lastly, we predict that the response times will increase and accuracy will decrease- the further away the orientation is from 0 degrees. The independent variables in this experiment are the letter R (2 types: normal or mirror) and the rotation/Orientation in degrees (8 levels).
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\5Long Labs\LL0\sample report LL0.docx

According to SDT, the subjects in a yes/no task base their response on the value that a decision variable achieves during each trial. If the decision variable is sufficiently high during a given trial, the subject responds yes (a signal was presented); otherwise, the subject responds no (no signal was presented). The value that defines sufficiently high is called the criterion .

For example, consider a psychologist attempting to determine whether or not a child has attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The psychologist might administer the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL; Achenbach & Edelbrock, 1983) and diagnose the child as having ADHD if the resulting score is 10 or higher (Rey, Morris- Yates, & Stanislaw, 1992).

If the subject is using an appropriate decision variable, and if the subject is capable of distinguishing between signals and noise, the decision variable will be affected by the stimuli that are presented. However, the criterion will also be exceeded on most noise trials, resulting in a high proportion of yes responses on noise trials (i.e., a high false-alarm rate). Thus, a liberal criterion biases the subject toward responding yes , regardless of the stimulus.

By contrast, a high, or conservative , value for the criterion biases the subject toward responding no , because the criterion will rarely be exceeded on signal or noise trials. This will result in a low false-alarm rate, but also a low hit rate. The only way to increase the hit rate while reducing the false-alarm rate is to reduce the overlap between the signal and the noise distributions.

Clearly, the hit and false-alarm rates reflect two factors: response bias (the general tendency to respond yes or no , as determined by the location of the criterion) and the degree of overlap between the signal and the noise distributions.

The latter factor is usually called sensitivity , reflecting the perceptual origins of SDT: When an auditory signal is presented, the decision variable will have a greater value (the stimulus will sound louder) in listeners with more sensitive hearing. The major contribution of SDT to psychology is the separation of response bias and sensitivity.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 1-signal detection theory\stanislawtodorovdprim1999_SDT.pdf

text: hearing. The major contribution of SDT to psychology is the separation of response bias and sensitivity. This point is so critical that we illustrate it with five examples from widely disparate areas of study. Our first example is drawn from perception, where higher thresholds have been reported for swear words than for neutral stimuli (Naylor & Lawshe, 1958).
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 1-signal detection theory\stanislawtodorovdprim1999_SDT.pdf

text: higher thresholds have been reported for swear words than for neutral stimuli (Naylor & Lawshe, 1958). A somewhat Freudian interpretation of this finding is that it reflects a change in sensitivity that provides perceptual “protection” against negative stimuli (Erdelyi, 1974). However, a false alarm is more embarrassing for swear words than for neutral stimuli. Furthermore, subjects do not expect to encounter swear words in a study and are, therefore, cautious about reporting them.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 1-signal detection theory\stanislawtodorovdprim1999_SDT.pdf

text: do not expect to encounter swear words in a study and are, therefore, cautious about reporting them. Thus, different apparent thresholds for negative than for neutral stimuli may stem from different response biases, as well as from different levels of sensitivity. In order to determine which explanation is correct, sensitivity and response bias must be measured separately. A second example involves memory studies.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 1-signal detection theory\stanislawtodorovdprim1999_SDT.pdf

text: sensitivity and response bias must be measured separately. A second example involves memory studies. Hypnosis sometimes improves recall, but it also increases the number of intrusions (false alarms). It is important, therefore, to determine whether hypnosis actually improves memory, or whether demand characteristics cause hypnotized subjects to report more memories about which they are uncertain (Klatzky & Erdelyi, 1985).
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 1-signal detection theory\stanislawtodorovdprim1999_SDT.pdf

The former explanation implies an increase in sensitivity, whereas the latter implies that hypnosis affects response bias. Again, it is important to measure sensitivity and response bias separately. Our third example involves a problem that sometimes arises when comparing the efficacy of two tests used to diagnose the same mental disorder.

SDT can solve this problem by determining the sensitivity of each test in a metric that is independent of the criterion (Rey et al., 1992).

SDT analyses (Thomas & Hogue, 1976) have shown that jury instructions regarding the definition of reasonable doubt affect response bias (the willingness to convict) rather than sensitivity (the ability to distinguish guilty from innocent defendants).

In his presidential address to the Radiological Society of North America, Garland (1949) noted that different radiologists sometimes classified the same X ray differently. Sensitivity and response bias are confounded by most performance measures, including the hit rate, the falsealarm rate, the hit rate “corrected” by subtracting the falsealarm rate, and the proportion of correct responses in a yes/no task.

One solution to this problem involves noting that sensitivity is related to the distance between the mean of the signal distribution and the mean of the noise distribution (i.e., the distance between the peaks of the two distributions in Figure 1). SDT states that d ′ is unaffected by response bias (i.e., is a pure measure of sensitivity) if two assumptions are met regarding the decision variable: (1) The signal and noise distributions are both normal, and (2) the signal and noise distributions have the same standard deviation. We call these the d ′ assumptions .

The assumptions cannot actually be tested in yes/no tasks; rating tasks are required for this purpose. Rating Tasks Rating tasks are like yes/no tasks, in that they present only one stimulus type during each trial. However, rather than requiring a dichotomous ( yes or no ) response, rating tasks require graded responses.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 1-signal detection theory\stanislawtodorovdprim1999_SDT.pdf

text: However, rather than requiring a dichotomous ( yes or no ) response, rating tasks require graded responses. For example, subjects in a study of jury decision making may rate each defendant on a scale of 1 ( most certainly guilty ) to 6 ( most certainly innocent ). These ratings can be used to determine points on a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, which plots the hit rate as a function of the false-alarm rate for all possible values of the criterion.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 1-signal detection theory\stanislawtodorovdprim1999_SDT.pdf

A rating task with r ratings determines r  1 points on the ROC curve, each corresponding to a different criterion. For example, one criterion distinguishes ratings of “1” from ratings of “2.” Another criterion distinguishes ratings of “2” from ratings of “3,” and so on.

The ROC area typically ranges from .5 (signals cannot be distinguished from noise) to 1 (perfect performance). Areas less than .5 may arise from sampling error or response confusion; the minimum possible value is 0.

The area under the ROC curve in Figure 2 equals .90; this includes both the large shaded region and the smaller gray regions. The ROC area can be interpreted as the proportion of times subjects would correctly identify the signal, if signal and noise stimuli were presented simultaneously (Green & Moses, 1966; Green & Swets, 1966, pp. 45–49).

Forced-Choice Tasks In a forced-choice task, each trial presents one signal and one or more noise stimuli. The subjects indicate which stimulus was the signal.

text: presents one signal and one or more noise stimuli. The subjects indicate which stimulus was the signal. Tasks are labeled according to the total number of stimuli presented in each trial; an m -alternative forced-choice ( m AFC) task presents one signal and m  1 noise stimuli. For example, a 3AFC task for the study of recognition memory presents one old item and two distractors in each trial. The subjects indicate which of the three stimuli is the old item.
source_file: Dr.Mishra-materials\materials\Lab course materials\4Short Labs\Lab 1-signal detection theory\stanislawtodorovdprim1999_SDT.pdf

text: and two distractors in each trial. The subjects indicate which of the three stimuli is the old item. Each stimulus in an m AFC trial affects the decision variable. Thus, each m AFC trial yields m decision variable scores. Subjects presumably compare these m scores (or their corresponding likelihood ratios) with each other and determine which is the largest and, thus, the most likely to have been generated by a signal.

If the cue was a plus sign (a neutral cue), the target appears half the time to the left of the fixation point and half the time to the right.

Part (b) Typical response times: Responses to valid cues are faster than responses to invalid cues, and responses to neutral cues are about midway between. (Adapted from Posner et al., 1978.) The results of this study, as shown in Figure 9.6b, were that the time required to press the button—the response time—was significantly shorter when the target followed a valid cue than when it followed an invalid cue, with the response time to targets following neutral cues somewhere in between.
